confidence_why: Bunn and Bunn 1970, the only first-hand phonology of the variety they recorded, put a single primary stress on the final high-toned syllable (or on the final low when the word has no high), while Evans and Stoakes 2005, working from one speaker of a different, higher-altitude variety, reanalyse Golin as a three-tone word-tone language with tone anchored on the rightmost mora and posit no word stress at all, though they allow that the Bunns' variety has a different 'tune' and may not yield to their reanalysis.

new_statements.quote: On the analysis we present here, Golin is a word-tone language with three contrasting tones – high, mid and low – associated at the level of the word (or perhaps the foot). Tones are attached to the rightmost mora of their domain, with a relatively constant pitch realization at that point, but more freedom in the rest of the domain, giving rise to considerable variation at the etic level of pitch contours over the word. [p. 3] ... The phonological contrast involves several tonal patterns (namely three), rather than just location as in a pitch-accent language. And by possessing several distinct tonal patterns, associated to a domain larger than the syllable, it is clearly a word- or foot-tone rather than a syllable-tone language. [p. 26]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Golin (Chris Kia Aina's variety) is a word-tone (or foot-tone) language with a three-way H/M/L contrast whose tone attaches to the rightmost mora of the word; the word-level prosodic contrast is a tonal pattern, not a location contrast, and the chapter posits no word stress at all. The only mentions of 'stress' are in Hayata's typology table (Russian, English as stress languages, p. 26) and in two footnotes by Lee (p. 35 fn. 8: vowel back-shift 'might depend, for instance, on prominence (e.g. stress, even tone?)'; p. 49 fn. 26), which leave prominence unanalysed.
new_statements.exceptions: The analysis is explicitly restricted to Kia's dialect and to nominal words (verbs excluded, p. 9, p. 7); the Bunns' earlier two-tone syllable-tone analysis (Bunn & Bunn 1970, Bunn 1974) is rejected for Kia's variety but the authors note the Bunns' variety has a different 'tune' and 'we cannot be certain whether the variety described by the Bunns would yield to reanalysis' (pp. 7, 26). Donohue (1997) listed Golin as a syllable-tone language on the Bunns' data; Evans & Stoakes say this is 'clearly not to be the case for Kia's variety' (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Evans & Stoakes 2005 describe the Golin of a single speaker, Chris Kia Aina ('Kia's dialect', p. 9), and restrict the tonal analysis to nominal words; they contrast it with the variety described by Gordon and Ruth Bunn (SIL, 1970/1974), which Kia said has a different 'tune'. Dom, described by Tida (2000, 2003) as a word-tone language, is noted as mutually comprehensible with Golin (p. 8).

tone_statements.translation: The data presented in this paper are basically all from the author's own fieldwork. For the Golin group I also refer to Bunn & Bunn (1970), Bunn (1974) and Evans et al. (2005), but for Bunn & Bunn (1970) and Bunn (1974) I use data reinterpreted, following Tida (2003b), as having the following three word tones: (8) High type: every syllable of the word has high pitch, e.g. gwí 'wind', díl 'pumpkin type', múrú 'all', níbíl 'sick'; Rising type: only the word-final syllable is high and the other syllables are low, e.g. puúl 'knife', digé 'armband', naalé 'locust', gilaá 'night', gumán 'nose'; Low type: every syllable of the word has low pitch, e.g. mo 'or', bol 'bed', keba 'sweet potato', gaan 'child'. [§2.4] The Simbu languages are probably all tone languages, in which melodies taking the word as their domain are distinctive.
